# The many faces of Skanda

No important name has only one face. **Skanda** appears ​as a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and a digital temple. This post looks at each face in ‌turn: the name and its roots, the Devanagari original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the symbols and sanctuaries, and the afterlife that brought the canonical spelling into the present.

## At a Glance

- ‌**Restored name:** Skanda
- **ASCII form:** skanda
- **Meaning:** "‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god of war who leads the divine hosts ​against the enemies of the gods."
- **Domain of influence:** War, Commander
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** स्कन्द (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Skanda** (*skanda*) — War, the Divine Hosts · ​‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "War, Commander". The name means "‘The ​Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god of war who leads the divine hosts against the enemies of the gods.".

**Skanda** is the ​Hindu war-god: the ever-youthful general of the devas’ hosts, born from the combined fire of Śiva’s third eye to destroy the demon Tāraka. Tamil India knows him as Murugan, ​the eternally beautiful mountain lord of the six abodes; the Sanskrit world as Kārttikeya, son of the Pleiades’ fosterage.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **स्कन्द**. Etymologically it means ​"‘The Attacker’ — a name of Kārttikeya, son of Śiva (or of Agni), the god of war who leads the divine hosts against the enemies of the gods.".

The ‌canonical spelling **Skanda** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *skanda* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. ## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **स्कन्द**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Skanda*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- ‌Sanskrit Skanda is written in Devanagari as स्कन्द
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath ​consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈskʌndə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Skanda).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Skan-** — The cluster sk is ​preserved; short a as in “cup”.
- **-da** — The name means “the Attacker”, “the Leaper” — a war-name, not a birth-name.
- **-n-** — The cluster sk is preserved in ​every period of the language; no sound is lost between the s and the k.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “SKUN-duh”

Kindred and historical forms of ​the name:

- **Form** — Kārttikeya
- **Form** — Murugan
- **Form** — Subrahmaṇya
- **Kumāra** — (all the same god)
- **Tamil** — Murukan

One god, six names per tradition — born of ​six sparks from the gods’ outraged eyes.

## Mythology

The Skanda myth is the war-god’s birth-saga: the gods, unable to defeat Tāraka, whose boon made him unkillable except by a son ‌of Śiva, contrived the god’s marriage to Pārvatī; the child was born as fire from the third eye, fostered by the Pleiades, and general of heaven before he was ​a week old. The Tamil Murugan traditions add the wooing of Vaḷḷi, the huntress, and the gnostic doctrine of the *Arupadaiveedu*, the six stations of grace.

### The Birth of ‌Fire (Kumāra Cycle)

When Agni and the river Ganges could not carry the god’s seed, they left it in the reeds of the Gangā’s bank; six infants were found ​there by the six Kṛttikā nymphs, each nursing one — until Pārvatī gathered them into a single six-headed child. His first week closed with the death of Tāraka, slain by ‌the spear his mother gave him.

### The Deva-Senāpati (Skanda Purāṇa)

The great Purāṇa bearing his name makes him general of the gods’ hosts and husband of Devasenā — ‘the ​army of the gods’ — a marriage arranged before his birth. His camp is on the world’s margin; his peacock mount, the demon Siṃhakeśin subdued, struts beneath his banner.

### ‌Vaḷḷi and Teyvāyāṉai (Murugan Cycle)

The Tamil epics tell how Murugan wooed the huntress Vaḷḷi in the guise of a tree-shade, and wed both her and Teyvāyāṉai, Indra’s daughter, ​in the great marriage at Tiruchendur. The legend’s two wives read theologically: divine grace (Teyvāyāṉai) and the soul’s own effort (Vaḷḷi) are both needed for union with the lord.

### The ‌Sage-Child (Subrahmaṇya Cycle)

As Subrahmaṇya — ‘the dear one to the Brahmins’ — he is the teacher-god, expounding the Vedas to his own father Śiva in the role of ​guru. The image flips the war-god into wisdom’s child, and fixes his southern temples as places of learning as much as of arms.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated ​with Skanda concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Divine General** — Commander of the gods’ armies — the deva-senāpati ‌— before whom no asura line holds.
- **Born of the Third Eye** — Six sparks from the gods’ wrath-eyes, fostered by the Kṛttikā — the Pleiades — as six infants, ‌fused into one.
- **The Spear** — Śakti, the lance his mother Umā gave him — one throw ended Tāraka, the boon-armed demon.
- **Lord of the Six Abodes** — Murugan’s ‌six mountain shrines from Tirupparankunram to Palani mark his Tamil country.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Skanda survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued ​below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

The six abodes (Ārupadaiveṭṭu) of Tamil Nadu are his living monuments; Gupta ​and Kushan sculpture give him his classical six-headed infant form. The Batu Caves of Malaysia, a modern Murugan shrine of cathedral scale, extend his geography into the diaspora.

## Realm ‌& Domain

## Across Cultures

Skanda is the great pan-Indian convergence: Vedic Rudra’s son, Tamil Murugan, Buddhist Kārttikeya ​of the north, and the Graha of the week’s Tuesday. The Greeks of the Northwest compared him to Ares and Mars; the Kushan coins show him as Skanda-Kumāra beside ‌the Buddha. His peacock entered Christian art’s immortality symbolism by the strangest of roads.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], ​and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

Murugan is Tamil country’s beloved god — the Kanda Ṣaṣṭhī festival at Tiruchendur draws millions, and the god’s hill-shrines anchor Tamil sacred geography. His six-headed ‌infant image, the Kārttikeya of Gupta art, defined the war-god’s iconography for Asia; and the Ṣaṣṭhī vow is observed across the subcontinent by parents of sons.

## A Meditation

Skanda: the war-name that means ‘the one who attacks’. In plain letters it reads like what it is — a battle-cry reduced to a name. ​The Tamil country still shouts it in festival; the lexicon keeps it here, at rest, its spear laid across the threshold of the temple.
